newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore police dismiss opposition poll complaint.
newsitem.headline: Singapore police dismiss opposition poll complaint.

text.p: Singapore police said on Friday that they had investigated and dismissed complaints by opposition political parties that election laws were broken during January general elections.

The police said they were advised by the Attorney-General's Chambers that none of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) members, including Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, had committed any offence as charged by the opposition parties.
After the January 2 elections, the Worker's Party and the Singapore Democratic Party filed five police reports alleging the PAP members had broken election laws.
They claimed the PAP candidates and non-candidates influenced voting at the polling stations by speaking to voters and shaking their hands.
However, the police statement said there was no evidence that PAP candidates had been trying to influence votes.

"As there is no evidence of canvassing or soliciting for votes or of any intention to do so, or of any efforts being made to persuade or dissuade anyone from voting for any particular candidate or party, no offence on the part of the 11 persons who had shaken hands or spoken with the voters has been disclosed," the police said in a statement.
The PAP won the election by a wide margin, taking all but two of parliament's 83 seats.

The PAP -- which has controlled Singapore since 1959 -- put on a tough campaign, saying wards voting for the opposition would be last in line for government goodies and charging prominent opposition candidate Tang Liang Hong with being a Chinese chauvinist who threatened racial harmony.

When Tang called the PAP leaders liars, they sued him for defamation. He fled the country after the election, saying he feared for his life. In May a court ordered Tang to pay Singapore $8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in damages to Goh and 10 other PAP leaders.
